report:
Reviewed **8 charts and all 18 flag entries**, counted from the HTML. Read both background documents. No files written; no gameplay tested. All numerical targets below are proposed playtest settings, not measured results. Cost estimates assume the existing flight and cockpit systems described in the research.

## 1. The whole loop

- **The mandatory circle makes exploration serve shopping.** Every find appears to require appraisal, sale/mortgage, and an upgrade before further exploration. Add explicit exits for continuing with cargo, keeping an appraised collectible, leaving without buying, and pursuing a clue immediately.
- **Fuel failure is attached only to refueling.** Travel also needs transitions to low fuel, unreachable destination, and stranding. Resolve these through one shared fuel state; otherwise each activity will invent different failure rules.
- **The main product is absent.** Add explicit transitions between manual flight, gambit flight, and pure screensaver/ORRERY viewing. Viewing must remain usable with a full hold, outstanding debt, or exhausted automation allowance.
- “Stranger places” is not a reward specification. The first upgrade needs a demonstrable destination or visible phenomenon it enables, rather than merely a larger number.

## 2. Signal hunt

- **Bearing plus a countdown can reduce the hunt to waiting.** Before departure, show signal class, uncertainty, estimated travel commitment, and fuel feasibility. Let players compare at least two leads; otherwise “worth chasing?” has no informed answer.
- The chart assumes every target requires an interstellar warp. Split same-system and other-system travel. Add cancel, temporarily unreachable, already discovered, and no-current-signals states.
- **“Stored,” “drop,” and “leave behind” lack onward transitions.** Dropping an item must return to the capacity decision; leaving a find should preserve its location. Separate data storage from physical artifact capacity so finding a mountain does not require throwing out a relic.
- Scanning needs an observable discovery moment: the feature becomes recognizable, the instrument explains what was unusual, and the record persists. An item name and price alone will not satisfy Max’s visual payoff.
- For the test, place the first recognizable discovery within **3 minutes**. Avoid repeated scans of the same body yielding new saleable copies.

## 3. Refuel: skim or dive

- **Safe infinite skimming may dominate diving**, particularly when automation can supply all fuel between manual sessions. Conversely, a deliberately tedious skim makes patience the price of safety. Start with a short skim yielding roughly **one ordinary jump**, and a successful dive yielding **three**, within tank capacity; measure voluntary choices.
- **The chart rewards waiting until a gauge threshold, not necessarily flying skill.** Exit momentum must matter, and the instrument must show a predicted safe-exit margin. If the collision barrier rescues every late exit, the risk is fictitious; its interaction needs testing.
- Add full tank, aborted approach, incompatible well, cooldown, and insufficient charge after failure. “Damage → back to flying” currently promises recovery without defining it.
- Use forced ejection and loss of that pass’s unbanked charge for the initial failure. Preserve previously held fuel and discoveries. This gives a readable consequence without adding hull repair and cargo destruction systems.
- Charge-rate and tolerance upgrades can erase the timing decision. Test each upgrade against both existing and newly accessible wells; do not make the baseline safety readout an upgrade purchase.

## 4. Stranded

- **Rescue has no guaranteed playable exit.** A broke ship towed to a settlement can still be empty and unable to earn. Rescue must include enough fuel to reach a known safe well, and the settlement must remain available when the time skip resolves.
- Show estimated rescue delay and bounty before entering stasis. Afterward, report elapsed galaxy time, new debt, and destination together. The skip should take seconds of player time.
- **Deliberately running dry can become return-to-town transport.** Compare the bounty and time cost against ordinary return travel. Repeated intentional rescue must carry a meaningful cost without confiscating the resources needed to resume exploration.
- “Can’t or won’t pay” makes borrowing the obvious choice if collection never happens. Define repayment and what happens at the debt limit. Recovery must remain possible even when another rescue is needed.

## 5. Cash in and upgrade

- **“True value” conflicts with changing local markets.** Reveal identity and an appraisal reference value, then separately display the current settlement’s offer. Otherwise price differences look like errors or dishonest appraisal.
- Per-item appraisal, sale, and upgrade clicks will become a return-trip chore. Batch common data; reserve individual reveal treatment for new artifact types. Add keep, repay, redeem collateral, decline purchase, and undock exits.
- **Mortgage is missing most of its lifecycle:** item ownership, repeat borrowing, carrying pledged cargo, sale restrictions, repayment, and default. A minimum version uses one pledged artifact in lender custody, a loan at **50% of appraisal**, and explicit redemption/forfeiture. Selling or pledging it elsewhere must be impossible; forfeiture must settle the associated loan.
- The five upgrade tracks demand five reasons to care and five balancing curves. The first test needs one engine upgrade with a visible destination payoff and one drive upgrade that changes an observed dive limitation.

## 6. Artifact clue chain

- **“Sell it: the clue goes with it” is a proposal to reject.** Once a player has read a clue, screenshots or memory bypass the intended sacrifice. Preserve learned information; selling gives up possession and collectible status, not knowledge.
- Region narrowing needs a finite search space. Start with **three candidate systems**, with observable traits that eliminate candidates. A vague region containing hundreds of procedural systems is labor, not deduction.
- Generation must guarantee an existing target, a viable route, and no prerequisite cycle. Add unreachable-for-now, discarded/sold artifact, duplicate clue, and completed-chain states. The current loop never concludes.
- **Every next remnant requires another appraiser visit.** Reveal enough field information to continue; appraisal can add interpretation and value. Otherwise the long arc is repeated commuting.
- Alien danger needs advance warning and a reversible response. Start with visible instrument interference and an option to leave the item at its recorded site; preserve safety gauges. Combat, pursuit, and destructive cargo interactions are separate systems.

## 7. Time economy

- **Define three different quantities:** galaxy date, accumulated personal time debt, and monetary debt. The chart makes them appear interchangeable. Display event costs before commitment and their consequences afterward.
- Inflation should reduce purchasing power through prices, not also subtract money from the wallet. Applying both would charge twice for the same effect.
- **Inflation can make borrowing advantageous.** In a hypothetical period with 10% inflation and 5% interest, a 100-unit loan becomes 105 nominal units but only **95.45** units of starting purchasing power. Combine this with appreciating collateral and repeated mortgages, and exploration becomes unnecessary. Specify rates and collateral rules together.
- A seeded price formula prevents random reload rerolls; it does not prevent predictable time-skipping for favorable prices. Include travel and time costs when testing market cycles, and prevent repeated appraisal from resetting collateral value or loan terms.
- Each arithmetic operation may be cheap. Explaining and balancing their combined effect on rescue, diving, and automation is not. Test one time event through all affected systems before adding continuous accumulation.

## 8. Screensaver hand-off

- **The cap is not actually defined.** Selling common data repeatedly bypasses hold capacity; a rare-lead buffer does not cap ordinary earnings unless filling it explicitly stops all earning. Define independent limits, initially **three pending leads and a fixed common-data value allowance**.
- Save allowance consumption across reloads and mode changes. Returning to the keyboard or clearing a notification must not reset it. Replenish through a completed manual expedition; no unlimited unattended earnings from toggling modes.
- A fixed 30% fuel rule cannot know whether the nearest well is reachable. Use route fuel plus reserve, with a safe fallback when no route exists.
- **First-match rules can starve later actions.** A nearby signal can repeatedly outrank “hold full.” Conditions must include action eligibility; scans need persistent completion records. Actions also need completion, cancellation, and emergency interruption rules to avoid constant target switching.
- At the cap, continue visual touring with economic progress paused. On return, show what changed, the active rule, and saved leads; allow immediate manual takeover during an action.

## Cross-loop problems

- **Refueling × rescue × economy:** a failed dive followed by rescue time, interest, inflation, repair, and artifact loss would punish one mistake through six channels. Start with the chosen dive penalty plus Max’s rescue time and bounty; defer additional loss systems.
- **Contemplation × time costs:** real-time interest makes watching a planet an economic mistake. Advance consequential galaxy time through explicit travel, dive, rescue, and productive-autopilot events. Pure viewing can animate a presentation state without advancing economic events or resetting allowances.
- **Automation × risk:** unlimited safe fuel and earnings would subsidize every manual gamble. Bound economic progress and test whether diving still attracts voluntary use after an unattended session.
- **Mortgages × clues:** preserving learned clues removes the proposed reason to mortgage for clue access. Mortgaging instead preserves collectible ownership for later redemption; test whether players value that enough before expanding the system.
- **Procedural breadth × visible discoveries:** generating coordinates is cheaper than making discoveries look different. Guarantee a small set of legible phenomena before scaling rarity or galaxy size.
- **Pillars × current decisions:** PILLARS describes a screensaver without inventory and gameplay isolation without backup. Max’s newer automation and rescue decisions take precedence. Keep inventory/lore management in gameplay panels, preserve unobstructed viewing, and resolve the document mismatch later.

## Answers to Claude’s flags

All **18 entries**, including statements rather than questions:

1. **Signal—range:** Keep bearing and distance; show uncertainty at long range so the readout helps orientation without immediately resolving the find.
2. **Signal—false leads:** Every deliberate signal chase should reveal something recordable or visibly distinctive; allow low monetary value, not empty trips, in the first test.
3. **Signal—detection scale:** Use coarse galaxy-map hints and precise in-system readings, giving both destination choice and local discovery a role.
4. **Refuel—overstress cost:** Forced ejection with loss of unbanked pass charge; it provides immediate feedback without a repair subsystem.
5. **Refuel—time dilation:** Link dives to galaxy time, but display the estimated increment before commitment; a hidden financial penalty prevents informed risk-taking.
6. **Refuel—lab first:** Yes; test repeated dives with the intended camera, controls, exit behavior, and collision barrier before economy integration.
7. **Stranded—wake location:** Tow to the nearest viable settlement with emergency fuel; waking stranded again is not recovery.
8. **Stranded—cargo payment:** Offer voluntary cargo sale at arrival, then pay the bounty; avoid a separate compulsory confiscation system.
9. **Cash-in—two reveals:** Keep field identity hints and settlement interpretation/value, while making the field discovery rewarding independently.
10. **Cash-in—appraiser availability:** Every settlement appraises in the first build; scarcity initially adds commuting more reliably than meaningful choice.
11. **Cash-in—unproven mortgages:** Prototype one collateral slot with the full repayment/default lifecycle; do not infer simplicity from the loan calculation.
12. **Artifacts—narrowing without waypoint:** Use three inspectable candidate systems and an optional stronger hint after repeated misses, preventing indefinite search.
13. **Artifacts—danger:** Use signaled, reversible instrument interference that spares navigation and fuel safety information; defer damage and pursuit.
14. **Time—seeded prices:** Use a bounded seeded formula, but test predictable travel/time cycles; determinism alone does not prevent arbitrage.
15. **Time—last layer:** Yes; integration and tuning are expensive even when the formulas are short, so establish enjoyable expeditions first.
16. **Gambits—ordered rules:** Use three editable first-match slots, visible active-rule feedback, and emergency interruption; players need to understand why an action won.
17. **Gambits—manual rare finds:** Save stable leads without expiration; manual retrieval stays meaningful without making time away create urgent obligations.
18. **Gambits—diving:** Skim only initially; unattended dives complicate risk, recovery, and the manual skill test.

## Top 5 improvements, ranked

1. **Build one complete 15-minute expedition — loops 1, 2, 5, 6. Cost: medium.** Two leads, one visible discovery, one appraisal, one upgrade, and a newly reachable sight. Fixes the absence of an end-to-end proof that exploration rewards attention.
2. **Validate the skim/dive decision — loop 3. Cost: medium.** One well type, projected exit margin, banked-charge feedback, and recoverable failure. Give each tester five attempts; record voluntary dives and whether they can explain a failure. Fixes gauge-watching and always-skim risk.
3. **Implement safe capped hand-off — loops 1, 7, 8. Cost: medium.** Three editable rules, persistent allowances, leads, takeover, and continued viewing after the cap. Test a full hold and unreachable well. Fixes farming and protects the main product.
4. **Close the rescue loop — loops 3, 4, 5. Cost: cheap.** Forced test stranding, quoted delay/bounty, settlement arrival, debt record, and emergency fuel. Require a broke player to resume exploration within **60 seconds** of rescue completion. Fixes recovery dead ends.
5. **Specify and probe financial transitions — loops 5, 7, 8. Cost: medium.** One collateral slot and explicit time-event accounting; exercise repeat pledging, sale of pledged cargo, default, reload, and mode toggling. Fixes duplication and arbitrage before adding more markets.

## Cut or defer for the first friends-and-family build

- **Defer live inflation, shifting markets, and mortgage lending.** Keep rescue debt recorded and time jumps visible. These remain intended features; combining them immediately would obscure whether discovery and diving work.
- **Cut spatial inventory packing, fragile cargo, hull repairs, and forced confiscation.** Use a small artifact slot list plus a data ledger; capacity choices survive without four additional interaction systems.
- **Defer exotic well grades, most upgrade tiers, and advanced scanner channels.** One well and two upgrade purchases can test the relevant decisions.
- **Defer long procedural clue chains and harmful alien behavior.** Use one seeded three-site chain with a conclusion and one inspectable alien specimen; rare spawning cannot reliably expose content during a short test.
- **Defer closed-application offline simulation and advanced rule editing.** Keep running-app automation, three player-editable rules, screensaver, and ORRERY in the test.

Watch **3–5 players individually**. Record time to first discovery, unexplained stalls, voluntary dives, completed expeditions, and successful hand-offs. Ask each to predict their next action’s outcome before explaining it. Do not treat these targets as evidence of fun until observed.
decisions: Treated Max’s current decisions as authoritative where the older PILLARS document differs.
Answered all 18 flag entries, including declarative research notes.
Presented numerical settings as provisional playtest targets, not observed results.
Distinguished first-playtest deferrals from removing features from the intended MVP.
Reviewed the supplied design and local research without independently verifying claims about reference games or auditing implementation code.

invariants: Screensaver and ORRERY remain the main product.
Preserve Max’s skim/dive choice, rescue and time debt, intended economy, artifact progression, and capped player-authored automation.
accepted_decisions: No new design decisions accepted by Max during this review; all recommendations remain proposals.
rejected_approaches: Removing learned clues on sale: screenshots and memory bypass the restriction.
Using storage alone to cap automation while allowing automatic sales: repeated selling bypasses the cap.
Treating seeded market prices as sufficient exploit prevention: predictable time and travel cycles remain possible.
Stacking repair, cargo loss, and existing rescue penalties before testing the dive: obscures risk tuning and expands scope.
unresolved: Actual fun and legibility of skim/dive under the current flight controls.
Approved economic clock, automation allowance renewal, mortgage/default rules, and rescue debt limits.
Which proposed first-playtest deferrals Max accepts.
checkpoint.next_action: Use Max’s feedback to revise the relevant charts and select the first playtest scope; do not treat these recommendations as approved implementation requirements.
